P1.evidence: No setter, no application referenced, so P1a drops out. The opening was consumed by a ten-minute audio failure and then small talk about the rep's surname and a Polish friend, after which the open question ran well: 'walk me through, like, what's been going on? Like, what's the main thing you're trying to fix right now in terms of your health, fitness?' No four-part frame was set and no agreement was taken, so the call had no agreed shape — which matters more than usual here, because a frame that includes 'what's in the way' is where a 70-year-old's medical history is supposed to be invited rather than stumbled upon.

P2.evidence: Five hits and three of the most consequential misses in the batch. The injury questioning was genuinely good and persistent — 'Apart from that, any other, anything that limits your movements?', then 'What's going on with the knee? What happened? What kind of injury?', then 'Any back pains', then 'Anything around the hip area and any stiffness, any pains?' — and it produced the ACL reconstruction, the meniscus damage, the retinal injury and the back pain. Health conditions were asked, which is why P2c scores a hit on the rubric: the rep asked and received 'No, no, no chronic conditions whatsoever.' What follows is the problem, and it is not a scoring problem but a judgement one. Twenty minutes later the prospect volunteered that a urologist had told him he probably had prostate cancer, that he had refused the biopsy, and that he was self-treating with ivermectin — directly contradicting the earlier answer — and the rep did not return to the question, revise anything, or acknowledge it. The check was run; the answer was overturned in front of him and he did not notice. Age, height and weight were never asked and only weight was volunteered. Occupation was never asked at all, which is why the fact that he is on Social Security supporting three daughters arrived at the price rather than in Baseline. Sleep and daily energy were never raised, on a 70-year-old competitive athlete whose stated problem is stamina and whose stated risk is overtraining.

P3.evidence: Some genuinely good work sitting next to a large hole. P3e ran properly and produced real material: 'when you think about it for a second, what would that moment be worth to you if you would actually achieve that? And compete with the top-notch?' And P3g landed the deepest moment on the call, when the rep took the prospect's own remark about his grandmother reaching 95 and reframed the whole purchase: 'competition is nice, it's cool, but it's playing the longevity game, being healthy, capable of doing things on your own when you're in your 90s too, right?' — which the prospect accepted. That is the right move made at the right time. The hole is P3f. This man has a wife and three daughters he is still supporting, and not once was he asked who else his health affects — despite the wife becoming the decisive obstacle twenty minutes later. Running P3f properly would have put her in the room as a beneficiary before she arrived as a blocker. The bridge question was also never asked; the why work here was all about the competition.

P4.evidence: Not attempted. The rep learned the history — swimming only, cycling abandoned after the retinal injury, a plateau lasting years — but never asked what he had tried in order to fix the plateau, what happened, why it did not stick, or what is actually in the way. The prospect's own answer was available and untouched: he does not train because gyms have never interested him and he had a bad experience the one time he swung a kettlebell alone. Nobody named that gap, so the offer was never positioned against it.

P5.evidence: Skipped for the seventh consecutive call in this batch, and skipped on the prospect where it was most available. He had already supplied the raw material himself — a hospitalisation that cost him last year's qualification, a body that can only manage two of four events, a five-month deadline, and a joke about competitors dying off around him. Not one consequence question was asked: no two-year picture, no willingness to settle, no why not, no line in the sand. When the price landed there was nothing behind it, which is why 'I'm not going to be able to make that' arrived as a flat refusal rather than as a problem to solve.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran and ran before the number, in a well-tailored form: 'Do you feel like if you had this right training and nutrition in check and the accountability from Trevor, all built around your life, do you agree that you would get to your goal and be in the best shape for the December competition?' The answer was soft — 'Yeah. It seems like those things would be good for me' — and that is where the phase failed. The script says move forward only on a clear yes, and 'it seems like those things would be good for me' is not one. P6b was never asked at all, so the prospect was never given the chance to name what would stop him, and the thing that stopped him ninety seconds later was money he would have disclosed if asked.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted so the phase applies, and effectively none of it ran. P11a is partial only in the narrowest sense: money moved, but a $100 refundable deposit against an undecided purchase is not collecting payment for the programme, and the rep had already committed to returning it on a no. The Trevor onboarding call was not scheduled — the only thing booked was another sales call. The agreement was never mentioned. The welcome email, the Skool community link and the onboarding questionnaire were never mentioned. The call ended with a prospect who had paid $100, agreed nothing, and been coached on what to tell his wife.

objection_plays.detail: 'Can I have a day to think about that?' is OA and it was not treated as its own objection — it was absorbed into the wife conversation and granted. The rep did run one adjacent move well earlier, the belief check, but none of the OA sequence followed: no 'what makes you feel it can', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'when do you make a different decision', no closing 'are you sure'. Given the prospect had just named a hard financial ceiling, granting the day was arguably the right commercial call; it is still not the play.

The most complete play execution anywhere in this batch, run close to the script. The obstacle question ran — 'have you spoke with your wife before about this? What's her approach to this?' — and got a real answer about limited income. The rep then pre-framed her objection for him: 'my concern is that her response is going to be, okay, so we want to do a fitness program for how much? Are you crazy?... Because she doesn't have all the context that we just talked about.' Then the consequence question, 'what would you do if she says no?', which drew out the ownership answer, 'at the end of the day, it's my decision', which the rep immediately reinforced: 'if this is your decision, that you can make this decision right now.' And then the scripted fallback executed exactly as written — 'let's put down like a $100 refundable deposit, you go to talk to her today, and we meet up tomorrow... If it's a yes, we move forward, if it's a no, I'll send you back immediately the $100.' Two scripted moves were skipped: the money-aside belief question and 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?', the second of which was the strongest card available given the medical history. The rep also went past the script in one respect, scripting the line for the prospect to use on his wife: 'you will say that, look, I already put down the deposit, I want to do it.'

Better framing than usual and no substance underneath it. The isolate ran cleanly — 'Just to triple check, finances aside, does this kind of check all the boxes for you?' And for the first time in this batch the manager's permission-and-worst-case framing ran close to verbatim: 'we don't have anything set in stone, like set payment plans, everything what we do... it's custom to what their abilities are in the current moment. In order for me to prepare that, we would need to have a discussion about what's possible, what's not possible... In the worst case, we can just create a game plan to work towards the future.' Then nothing. Not one financial-picture item was asked — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus after bills, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments. Having invited the honest conversation, the rep did not have it; he went straight to proposing $1,200 for a first month to a man who had just said his ceiling was around $500 and that he is on Social Security supporting three daughters. The scripted discussion he offered would have established within two minutes that the number did not exist.

No timing objection. Timing ran the other way — a November qualification and December state meet gave the purchase a natural deadline, which the rep used well: 'We have July, August, September, October, and some November, which is almost five months. That's enough time.'

No fear or doubt about the method or the coach. He had already used the free videos and bought a kettlebell. The one thing that should have been treated as apprehension — 'A little worried on some of them, I locked myself out with a kettle ball because of, you know, swinging it around' — was answered with a description of the form-check process rather than engaged as a concern, but it was not raised as an objection.

The clinical script gap, in its most acute form in the corpus. A 70-year-old disclosed an unresolved prostate cancer question with a declined diagnostic biopsy, self-administered ivermectin, a September review pending, a reconstructed ACL, meniscus damage, a retinal repair, back pain, a hospitalisation caused by overtraining before last year's race, and a prior injury from swinging a kettlebell unsupervised. The playbook contains no screening question, no clearance requirement, no escalation route and no disqualification rule for any of it. The rep had nothing to reach for and reached for nothing — the cancer disclosure was followed immediately by 'Okay, okay, cool. So, but do you have, like, a dream to compete in January with the best?' This is the gap already logged against the Tyron Giuliani call, and this call shows it failing in the more dangerous direction: there the clinical reality lost a well-funded deal, here it was not noticed at all.

Second script gap, commercial. This prospect is on a fixed income with a stated ceiling of roughly $500 against a $6,000 price — a structural affordability gap, not a liquidity one, and one no payment plan closes. The playbook's OC assumes latent capacity that can be surfaced; it has no disqualification path and no lower-tier product to route to. The prospect identified the gap himself and asked for the product that does not exist: 'maybe Trevor should consider when people are at my, maybe, you know, senior plan.' The rep's answer was 'I'll let him know.' Note that the 07/06 team meeting confirms a $200/month Primal University tier does exist and that reps are told to route unaffordable prospects into it — that route was not offered here.

notes: The objection handling was the best in the batch and the qualification underneath it was the worst — OB was run almost to the letter on a man whose real blocker was a fixed income, and whose medical disclosure should have stopped the sale before price was ever discussed. The single coachable moment is at the cancer disclosure: the rep's next sentence was about the January competition. Everything downstream, including the deposit, follows from not stopping there.
